title: How does indexing work internally (B-tree for range queries, hash index for exact match, clustered vs non-clustered)?
shortTitle: How indexing works internally — B-tree for range queries, hash index for exact match, clustered vs non-clustered

s1_definition.profdef: Internally, most relational indexes are B-tree (more precisely B+tree) structures: a shallow, high-fanout, self-balancing tree where internal nodes hold separator keys and leaf nodes hold the indexed values in sorted order, chained together for efficient range scans. A hash index instead stores keys in hash buckets, giving average O(1) equality lookups but no ordering, so it cannot serve range or sort operations. A clustered index stores the actual table rows in the leaf nodes in key order, so the index is the table; a non-clustered index stores only the key plus a locator (the primary key or a physical row id) and requires a second lookup to fetch the full row.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India account directory. A B+tree is like a multi-level filing cabinet: the top drawer says "accounts A–M in cabinet 1, N–Z in cabinet 2," inside cabinet 1 the folders say "A–F here, G–M there," and the bottom folders hold the actual sorted account cards linked side by side so you can flip through a range easily. A hash index is like a coat-check: you hand over account SAV2001, a machine instantly computes "bucket 47," and your coat is there — lightning fast for one exact ticket, but useless if you ask "give me all coats from tickets 2000 to 3000," because the buckets are scattered with no order.
s1_definition.oneliner: B-tree keeps keys sorted so it wins at ranges and sorting; a hash scatters keys so it only wins at single exact-match lookups.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Internally, most relational indexes are B-tree (more precisely B+tree) structures: a shallow, high-fanout, self-balancing tree where internal nodes hold separator keys and leaf nodes hold the indexed values in sorted order, chained together for efficient range scans. A hash index instead stores keys in hash buckets, giving average O(1) equality lookups but no ordering, so it cannot serve range or sort operations. A clustered index stores the actual table rows in the leaf nodes in key order, so the index is the table; a non-clustered index stores only the key plus a locator (the primary key or a physical row id) and requires a second lookup to fetch the full row.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India account directory. A B+tree is like a multi-level filing cabinet: the top drawer says "accounts A–M in cabinet 1, N–Z in cabinet 2," inside cabinet 1 the folders say "A–F here, G–M there," and the bottom folders hold the actual sorted account cards linked side by side so you can flip through a range easily. A hash index is like a coat-check: you hand over account SAV2001, a machine instantly computes "bucket 47," and your coat is there — lightning fast for one exact ticket, but useless if you ask "give me all coats from tickets 2000 to 3000," because the buckets are scattered with no order.

**One line to remember:** B-tree keeps keys sorted so it wins at ranges and sorting; a hash scatters keys so it only wins at single exact-match lookups.

sections.s2_technical:
A B+tree stays balanced, meaning every leaf is the same depth from the root, so a lookup always costs the same small number of disk reads. Fanout is high — a single 8 kilobyte page can hold hundreds of keys — so even a billion-row table is only three or four levels deep. That is why a primary-key lookup on two hundred million accounts touches perhaps four pages, not two hundred million rows.

The key property for banking reports is that B+tree leaves are sorted and linked. When the statement query asks `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31'`, the tree navigates to the first qualifying leaf and then walks the linked leaves in order until it passes the upper bound. Range queries, `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`, and `MIN`/`MAX` all exploit this ordering.

A hash index applies a hash function to the key to pick a bucket. Equality lookups like `WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001'` are average constant time, often faster than a B-tree for pure point lookups. But a hash destroys ordering: there is no concept of "the next key," so `WHERE balance > 500000` or `ORDER BY created_at` cannot use it. PostgreSQL supports `USING hash`, but most teams default to B-tree because it serves both equality and range, whereas hash only serves equality.

The clustered versus non-clustered distinction is about where the row data lives. In a clustered index the leaf nodes are the rows themselves, physically ordered by the key, so reaching the leaf gives you the whole row with no extra hop. A non-clustered index leaf holds only the indexed columns plus a pointer. To get the other columns the engine performs a second lookup — in InnoDB it looks up the clustered index by primary key, and in PostgreSQL it fetches the heap tuple by physical location. That extra hop is the "bookmark lookup," and avoiding it is exactly why covering indexes exist. A senior nuance: because a non-clustered index in InnoDB stores the primary key as its row locator, a large primary key bloats every secondary index, which is one reason banks prefer compact keys.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a quarterly statement job: "all transactions for account SAV2001 between January and March." This is a range query on a sorted dimension, and it is exactly what a B+tree is built for — seek to the start date, then walk the sorted leaves until the end date.

Problem 2 — The authentication service does millions of "look up this exact session token" calls per minute and never asks for ranges. This is a pure equality workload, and it is exactly where a hash index can shine.

Problem 3 — The statement query also needs the amount and direction, not just the date. If the index only holds the date, the engine must hop back to the table for every row. This is exactly the clustered-versus-non-clustered cost, and it motivates thinking about what the leaf actually stores.

The mini-project builds a statement service. We create a transactions table with a B+tree composite index for the range query and a separate table of session tokens with a hash index for exact-match lookups. The service runs both a range scan and a point lookup and logs which access path each uses.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/index-internals-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Prove the B+tree does a range scan
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions
  WHERE account_id='SAV2001' AND created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31';"
# Expect: Index Scan using ix_txn_acct_date

# Prove the hash index does an exact match
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM session_tokens WHERE token='abc123...';"
# Expect: Index Scan using hx_session_token
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the statement job asks for SAV2001 transactions from 1 January to 31 March 2026.

Step 1 — The service calls `findByAccountIdAndCreatedAtBetween`, which becomes a SQL query with a `BETWEEN` range on `created_at` scoped to one account.

Step 2 — The planner picks the B+tree `ix_txn_acct_date`. It descends from the root through one or two internal levels to the leaf holding the first entry where account is SAV2001 and date is on or after 1 January.

Step 3 — Because leaves are sorted and linked, the engine walks forward along the chain reading TXN001 then TXN002. When it reaches TXN003 dated 1 May, that is past 31 March, so it stops immediately — no wasted reads.

Step 4 — The two qualifying entries point to the full rows, which are returned as the statement.

Step 5 — Separately, the auth service calls `validateToken`. The hash index hashes the token string to a bucket number, jumps straight to that bucket, and either finds the single matching row or returns empty. No tree traversal, no ordering.

```text
2026-10-25 13:50:02 INFO  StatementService - B+tree RANGE scan: account SAV2001 from 2026-01-01T00:00 to 2026-03-31T23:59
2026-10-25 13:50:02 INFO  StatementService - Hash EXACT-MATCH lookup for token prefix abc123...
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  RANGE QUERY (B+tree)                      EXACT MATCH (Hash)
  account=SAV2001, Jan–Mar                  token=abc123...
    │                                         │
    ▼                                         ▼
  B+tree root                               hash(token) → bucket 47
    │ descend internal nodes                  │
    ▼                                         ▼
  Leaf (SAV2001, 2026-01-15) ──linked──▶     bucket 47 holds 1 row
  Leaf (SAV2001, 2026-02-20)                  │
    │ stop at 2026-05-01 (> Mar)              ▼
    ▼                                       SessionToken row
  2 rows → statement                        1 row → valid session
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Index Internals ═══

  ┌─ Design decision ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  B+tree for transactions  → range, ORDER BY, GROUP BY     │
  │  Hash for session_tokens  → equality only, O(1) average   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── B+tree structure ──
  [root: A–M | N–Z]
      │
  [internal: A–F | G–M]
      │
  [leaf: (SAV2001,Jan)⇄(SAV2001,Feb)⇄(SAV2001,May)]  ← sorted + linked

  ── Hash structure ──
  hash(token) → bucket[0..N]
  bucket 47 → [ {token, account_id, issued_at} ]      ← no order

  ── Clustered vs non-clustered ──
  Clustered leaf  = full row (no extra hop)
  Non-clustered   = key + locator → 2nd lookup (bookmark)

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Service.quarterlyStatement(SAV2001, Jan, Mar)
  2.   → Repo.findByAccountIdAndCreatedAtBetween(...)
  3.     → B+tree seek + leaf walk → 2 rows
  4. Service.validateToken(abc123)
  5.   → Repo.findByToken(abc123)
  6.     → hash bucket → 1 row
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Internally, almost every relational index is a B+tree, which is a shallow, self-balancing tree with very high fanout. Because it is balanced, every lookup costs the same small number of page reads even on a billion-row table, and because the leaf nodes store the keys in sorted order and are linked together, the B+tree is excellent not just for equality lookups but for range queries, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, and MIN or MAX. A hash index is the other common structure: it hashes the key straight to a bucket, giving average constant-time equality lookups, but it throws away all ordering, so it cannot serve ranges or sorts at all.

The clustered versus non-clustered distinction is about where the actual row lives. In a clustered index the leaf nodes are the rows themselves, physically ordered by the key, so reaching the leaf gives you the whole row. A non-clustered index leaf holds only the indexed columns plus a pointer back to the row, so fetching the remaining columns costs a second lookup, which is exactly the overhead a covering index removes.

At the National Bank of India I used both deliberately. The quarterly statement job runs a date range for one account, so I used a composite B+tree on account id and created-at; the planner seeks to the start date and walks the sorted leaves until it passes the end date, reading nothing extra. The authentication service, on the other hand, only ever does exact token lookups millions of times a minute and never asks for a range, so a hash index was a good fit there.

The nuance I always raise is that in InnoDB every secondary index stores the primary key as its row locator, so a bloated primary key quietly makes every other index larger and slower, which is one more reason banks prefer compact, time-ordered keys. And as always I confirm the chosen access path with EXPLAIN ANALYZE rather than assuming.
